newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin sees declining jobless rate.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin sees declining jobless rate.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Monday that Canada is entering a long period of sustained growth that over time will lower its chronically high unemployment rate.
"Just as the unemployment rate has been ratcheted up for the last 20 years ... you are going to see it steadily ratcheting down over the next 20 years," Martin told reporters at a press conference.
Martin said he thinks that over time Canada will make up a "substantial portion" of the gap in economic growth rates and unemployment rates between Canada and the United States.

Many economists expect Canada's real gross domestic product to grow by 3 percent and higher in 1997, better than the 2.6 percent growth rate forecast for the U.S. economy this year. Through the 1990s, Canada's GDP growth has lagged that of the United States.

During that period, the unemployment rate has been substantially higher in Canada than in the United States. Figures for January showed unemployment at 9.7 percent in Canada, compared with 5.4 percent for the United States.

Martin said he expects Canada's consumer sector, wary of spending because of high household debt levels and job uncertainty though the 1990s, will give the Canadian economy a shot in the arm this year. "We've had a one-legged recovery in Canada. Primarily, it has been export-oriented, and I think we are now beginning to see the signs of a domestic pickup, and that domestic pickup is going to have a very strong effect on job creation," he said.
But Martin declined to make a definitive forecast of when Canada's unemployment rate could slip under nine percent.

Martin said he expects economic growth in Quebec and the Maritime provinces to rebound closer to the national rate, but alluded to "particular circumstances" in Quebec that he said are inhibiting economic growth.

French-speaking Quebec is headed by a separatist government that in October 1995 narrowly lost a referendum on the province's separation from Canada, and which has promised to hold another referendum. Most economists expect Quebec's economic growth to continue to lag the national average in 1997. Securities dealer Levesque Beaubien Geoffrion Inc, for example, expects Quebec's economy to grow by only 2.6 percent in 1997, compared with a Canadian average of 3.6 percent.
